title: COP31 flop triggers backlash in Australia; Pacific nations express despair
html:
Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen speaks to the journalists at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey on Nov 20.

PHOTO: REUTERS

SYDNEY/ANTALYA, Turkey – The finger-pointing to assign blame for the collapse of UN climate talks in Turkey began on Nov 23 with calls for the resignation of the Australian minister leading them, while the Pacific island nations most at risk expressed their despair over the failure of countries to collectively address global warming.

For the first time since the 2009 meeting in Copenhagen, the COP climate conference could not reach a final agreement from its talks after the EU and others rejected a final deal that did not include any mention of the role of fossil fuels in global warming because of pressure from Saudi Arabia and other oil-producing nations.

This was the first meeting since the UN’s environmental body confirmed global temperatures were set to exceed the 1.5 deg C level scientists have said will cause extreme weather impacts to intensify, and the lack of collective action has increased a sense of impotence around the multilateral COP process.

Turkey hosted the latest talks, called COP31, in Antalya, but shared leadership with Australia.

Australian Energy Minister Chris Bowen was the COP31 president of negotiations, and opposition politicians in his home country blamed him for the failure.

“This energy minister has got to go because he is a complete and utter failure,” Angus Taylor, a Member of the Australian Parliament who leads the opposition, told reporters on Nov 23.

“Chris Bowen was responsible for it. He should go,” Taylor said.

Speaking after the COP31 talks, Bowen blamed the very strong red lines many parties had on climate change.

Inside the Australian Parliament, other opposition members asked Prime Minister Anthony Albanese why he would not sack Bowen after the country had spent A$150 million (S$128 million) on COP31.

Albanese did not comment directly on whether he would ask Bowen to step down.

“We believe that climate change is real. We believe in the science,” he said.

“Whether it is environmental security or national security, we act in Australia’s national interest.”

Multilateral process

The COP31 talks began on Nov 9, but the lack of a final agreement extended the summit to a record overtime on Nov 22.

There was already some contention before the summit started as Australia, which has been at the forefront of efforts to act against global warming, fought with Turkey over hosting duties.

More than 190 countries were represented, and more than 92,000 people had registered, making it provisionally the largest UN climate conference on record. The United States did not send a delegation.

The 2025 talks in Belem, Brazil, produced a deal but no commitment to phase out fossil fuels.

Li Gao, the vice-minister of China’s Ministry of Ecology and Environment and head of its COP31 delegation, expressed disappointment over the failure to reach a consensus on the final statement.

That fight meant “we missed lots of things that a lot of developing countries want”, he said.

“We cannot see this as a failure of this multilateral process. We believe that it reminds us we need to try to further the multilateral process to get the consensus,” he added.

Bhupender Yadav, who led India’s delegation at COP31, said India engaged constructively and tirelessly with the presidencies and other parties.

“While concerns remain over certain elements of the cover decision, we remain committed to dialogue and constructive engagement until the very end to build consensus,” he said.

Most Pacific island nations, which are facing rising sea levels and other existential threats from climate change, expressed deep disappointment.

“We have been let down on all sides,” the delegation from the Marshall Islands at COP31 said in a statement. REUTERS
summary: Turkey hosted the latest talks, called COP31, in Antalya but shared leadership with Australia.
